title: Topology, open and closed sets, and neighborhoods
terms: topology; topological space; open set; closed set; neighborhood; standard topology.

exposition.text:
A topology T on X contains ∅ and X, is closed under arbitrary unions, and is closed under
finite intersections. Its members are open; a set is closed when its complement is open. A neigh-
borhood of x contains an open set containing x and need not itself be open. In the standard
topology on R, an open set contains a small interval about each of its points.
Arbitrary intersections of closed sets and finite unions of closed sets are closed. A set can be
both open and closed, or neither. To find the smallest topology containing specified sets, repeat-
edly add their finite intersections and arbitrary unions; on a finite underlying set this process
terminates.

question.text:
Let X = {a, b, c, d}. How many sets belong to the smallest topology on X containing {a, b} and
{b, c}?
(A) 4 (B) 5 (C) 6 (D) 7 (E) 8

solution.text:
Intersection adds {b} and union adds {a, b, c}. Together with ∅, X and the two original
sets these give six sets. Their unions and intersections add nothing further.

question.text:
Let X = {a, b, c} with topology {∅, {a}, {a, b}, X}. What is the closure of {b}?
(A) {b} (B) X (C) {b, c} (D) {c} (E) {a, b}

solution.text: The closed sets are X, {b, c}, {c}, ∅. Intersecting those that contain b gives {b, c}.

question.text:
In the usual topology on R, let N = [−1, 1] ∪ {2}. For exactly which real x is N a neighborhood
of x?
(A) x ∈ N (B) x ∈ [−1, 1] (C) x ∈ (−1, 1) (D) x ∈ {−1, 1, 2} (E) No real x

solution.text:
A neighborhood must contain an open interval about the point. This holds at every
x ∈ (−1, 1). Every interval about −1 or 1 includes points just outside N, and every interval
about the isolated member 2 does too. A neighborhood need not itself be open, but merely
belonging to it is insufficient.
